response.title: Do I need a 3D printer that heats the inside of its enclosure to print ABS and ASA parts that don't warp, or is a closed box enough?
response.answer:
No, you don't need an actively heated chamber to print ABS or ASA without warping. A fully enclosed printer with a passively heated chamber is often sufficient, especially for small and medium-sized parts.

However, an actively heated chamber makes a significant difference for large parts, tall parts, and parts with thick walls.

Passive vs. actively heated chambers

Chamber type

	

Typical chamber temperature

	

ABS / ASA performance




Open printer

	

20–30°C

	

High warping risk




Enclosed, unheated

	

35–45°C

	

Good for smaller parts




Well-insulated enclosure

	

45–55°C

	

Good for many medium parts




Actively heated

	

55–70°C

	

Better for large, demanding parts




Industrial heated chamber

	

70–90°C+

	

Best for challenging geometries and dimensional stability

These are approximate temperatures; actual passive chamber temperatures depend heavily on bed temperature, insulation, printer size, and ambient conditions.

Why chamber temperature matters

ABS and ASA shrink as they cool. If the bottom of your print stays hot while the upper layers cool too quickly, internal stresses develop.

These stresses can cause:

Warping: Corners lift off the build plate.

Layer splitting: Layers separate, especially on tall prints.

Dimensional inaccuracies: Parts deform as they cool.

Cracking: Internal stresses exceed the material's strength.

A warm chamber reduces temperature differences throughout the print.

How much difference does active heating make?

Approximate practical guidance

Passive chamber

40–50°C

Often sufficient for everyday ABS/ASA parts

Actively heated

60–70°C

More reliable for larger, taller parts

For example:

50 × 50 × 50 mm ABS part: A passive enclosure is usually fine.

150 × 150 × 100 mm ASA part: A passive enclosure at 45–50°C can work well, depending on geometry.

250 × 250 × 200 mm ABS part: Active chamber heating becomes much more valuable.

Large, flat ABS parts: Can warp even in a heated chamber because geometry and bed adhesion matter enormously.

These are guidelines, not guaranteed size thresholds.

How to get good results without active chamber heating

Preheat the enclosure: Set the bed to 100–110°C and let the chamber warm for 15–30 minutes before printing.

Aim for 45–50°C chamber temperature if your printer can reach it safely.

Avoid drafts: Keep the enclosure closed during printing.

Use appropriate bed adhesion: A suitable PEI surface, adhesive, or brim can help.

Minimize part cooling: ABS and ASA generally need much less cooling than PLA.

Allow gradual cooling: Don't immediately open the enclosure after printing.

Also, ABS and ASA emit ultrafine particles and VOCs during printing. An enclosure helps contain emissions but does not eliminate exposure; use appropriate exhaust ventilation or effective filtration. Make sure the printer's electronics, motors, and other components are rated for the chamber temperatures you intend to use.

My recommendation

If you're buying a printer primarily for ABS and ASA:

A passive enclosure that reliably reaches 45–50°C is a very reasonable choice. You don't necessarily need to pay extra for active chamber heating.

But if you frequently print large functional parts, particularly ones spanning 200 mm or more, I would favor an actively heated chamber capable of maintaining approximately 60–65°C.

One question: What's the approximate size of the ABS/ASA parts you want to print? For example, 100 mm, 200 mm, or 300 mm across? That makes a substantial difference in whether active heating is worth paying for.
